blocks.text: A point update in a Fenwick tree means changing the value at ONE single array index and propagating that change to every Fenwick node whose range includes that index. This is distinct from a range update, which changes many indices at once, covered in a separate topic. This lesson goes deep specifically on the point update mechanics, assuming you already understand the general Fenwick tree structure and the lowbit trick from the introduction topic.

The single most important idea in this topic: a point update propagates a DELTA (a change amount), never the raw new value directly. Every Fenwick node stores a partial SUM over a range, not the value at one position, so only a delta can be correctly combined into that stored sum.

blocks.caption: Starting at index 3 in an 8 element Fenwick tree, repeatedly adding lowbit visits indices 3, 4, then 8, before exceeding the array size and stopping.

blocks.text: Starting at index i, repeatedly add the lowbit of i to i, moving to i + lowbit(i), then that result plus its own lowbit, and so on, until i exceeds the array size. Every node visited along this walk gets its stored value increased by the delta.

The lowbit of a number is its lowest set bit, computed as i & (-i) in two's complement arithmetic. Adding lowbit to an index always moves toward larger indices, which is exactly why the update walk terminates once i exceeds the array size, there is nowhere further to propagate.

content.title: 2. Why a Delta, Not the New Value

blocks.text: Each Fenwick node at index i stores the sum of a specific range of the underlying array, not a single element's value. If a caller wanted to set index 3 to a brand new value directly, simply overwriting every visited node with that new value would be wrong, since those nodes' sums also include OTHER array elements beyond just index 3.

The correct approach: compute delta as (newValue minus the CURRENT value at that index), then ADD that delta to every node visited during the update walk. This way each node's stored sum shifts by exactly the right amount to reflect the one element that changed, without disturbing the contributions of every other element folded into that same node.

Consider an 8 element array with a Fenwick tree already built. Updating index 3 by delta = +5 visits exactly three nodes: index 3, index 4, and index 8, following the lowbit chain (3 + lowbit(3) = 3+1 = 4, then 4 + lowbit(4) = 4+4 = 8, then 8 + lowbit(8) = 8+8 = 16, which exceeds size 8, so the walk stops).

At each visited node, the stored value increases by exactly 5: tree[3] += 5, tree[4] += 5, tree[8] += 5. Every other node in the tree, index 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, is left completely untouched, since none of their ranges include index 3.
This is the entire point update function in isolation, deliberately minimal. The loop condition i <= n and the increment i += i & (-i) together implement the full lowbit walk described above.

Each point update runs in O(log n) time, since the number of indices visited during the lowbit walk is bounded by the number of bits in the array size, an array of size n visits at most log2(n) nodes before the index exceeds n.

content.title: 6. Update by Delta vs Set to a Value

blocks.text: Callers often want to SET index i to a new value directly, rather than think in terms of deltas. This requires two steps: first determine the CURRENT value at index i (either by maintaining a separate raw array alongside the Fenwick tree, or by querying a length one range sum), then compute delta as newValue minus that current value, and finally call the same update(i, delta) function shown above.

This two step pattern, query the current value first, then update by the computed delta, is a common point of confusion for anyone approaching Fenwick trees for the first time, and worth internalizing explicitly since nearly every real problem interface (like LeetCode's "update(index, val)") expects set semantics, not delta semantics.

Passing the new value directly into update() instead of the delta: this silently corrupts the tree, since it double counts or under counts depending on whether the new value happens to be larger or smaller than the old one, and the bug will not throw any error, just produce wrong query results later.

Forgetting Fenwick trees are commonly implemented 1-indexed: calling update with index 0 will not work correctly since lowbit(0) is 0, which would cause the loop to spin forever, since i += 0 never advances i past the loop condition.

Off by one errors between the caller's 0-indexed array and the Fenwick tree's internal 1-indexed array: a caller working with a standard 0-indexed array must remember to call update(i + 1, delta), not update(i, delta), when updating the array element at position i.

Range Sum Query Mutable is the canonical problem requiring point updates, since it explicitly requires updating individual elements while still supporting range sum queries efficiently, exactly the combination this topic and its sibling prefix sum query topic together solve.
